enrichment.short_title: Liu v SSHD: China's one-child policy and refugee particular social group
key_facts: A Chinese woman forcibly subjected to late-term abortion and threatened with sterilisation after refusing to comply with population-control officials fled to the UK and claimed asylum.
An adjudicator allowed her appeal on asylum and Article 3 grounds; the Secretary of State accepted the human rights decision but appealed on asylum to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal.

The IAT overturned the asylum finding, holding that 'women of child bearing age in China' was too wide and that a narrower group defined by persecution would not exist independently of the persecution feared.
On appeal Maurice Kay, Rix and Ward LJJ held the IAT erred by applying the 'independent existence' principle without Lord Steyn's qualification from Shah and Islam.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision reversing an adjudicator's grant of asylum; human rights leave to remain already accepted.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to a differently constituted IAT to reconsider whether the appellant had a well-founded fear of persecution for membership of a particular social group.
enrichment.ratio: The principle that a particular social group must exist independently of persecution does not defeat a group identified by immutable or fundamental characteristics where persecutory conduct may identify or cause its creation; the IAT must apply Lord Steyn's Shah and Islam qualification and consider Commonwealth jurisprudence on parents resisting China's reproductive controls.
legal_issues: Whether women resisting China's one-child policy constitute a particular social group under the Refugee Convention
Whether the IAT erred by defining the postulated group solely by reference to persecution
Application of Shah and Islam and Cheung/Chan/Applicant A authorities to reproductive-control cases
Whether the court should decide the social group issue finally or remit to the specialist tribunal

Cheung v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) [1993] 2 FC 314
Applicant A v Minister for Immigration and Ethnic Affairs (1997) 190 CLR 225

enrichment.short_title: Taefi v Jeffrey Green Russell: permission to appeal solicitor negligence
key_facts: Mr Taefi sued his former solicitors over handling of a default judgment in a rent arrears claim brought by Pegasi Management Company Ltd.
After default judgment the solicitors set it aside on an arguable defence that Pegasi had contracted with someone other than Taefi, but Taefi later accepted liability for the rent.
The negligence claim alleged failure to file an acknowledgment of service and insistence on costs that prevented settlement once Pegasi would have accepted principal only.
An attendance note suggested Mr Webster had proposed claiming the firm's costs, creating a factual dispute central to the second allegation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal from a trial finding of no negligence/causation in a solicitor negligence action.
enrichment.outcome: Longmore LJ granted qualified permission on grounds 1–9 subject to replacement of grounds 10–11; refused permission on grounds 10–11 as originally drafted; estimated hearing one-and-a-half days.
enrichment.ratio: Where negligence, causation and related factual disputes on an attendance note are arguable and interlinked, permission to appeal may be granted even though success could necessitate a retrial.
legal_issues: Whether there is a real prospect of success on failure to acknowledge service and default judgment
Whether the solicitor negligently insisted on recovery of costs preventing settlement
Whether causation was wrongly assessed because the defence was ultimately false
Whether grounds challenging findings on the underlying lease should be reframed

enrichment.short_title: Simms v Law Society: strike-off for dishonest high-yield investment work
key_facts: Mr Simms, former senior partner of Bower Cotton, faced OSS proceedings after over $50 million passed through client account in suspected prime-bank and high-yield investment schemes.
The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal found conduct unbefitting a solicitor including dishonesty in Hackar, Maxhurst and related transactions and ordered strike-off.
Issues included use of legally privileged documents, adjournment costs, and whether the solicitor honestly enquired into bogus bank guarantees and investment programmes.
The Divisional Court reheard the evidence and upheld findings that the appellant knowingly misled clients and retained undisclosed fees.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal by way of re-hearing from a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal strike-off order and related interlocutory costs orders.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; strike-off upheld; tribunal costs orders affirmed; residual costs issues adjourned for written submissions.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor who lends his authority to transactions he knows or should suspect are bogus or dishonest, and who dishonestly misleads clients about fees and representation, is properly struck off; privilege challenges do not prevent the tribunal considering disclosed material on re-hearing.
legal_issues: Procedural fairness of the disciplinary proceedings
Admissibility and use of legally privileged documents
Whether the solicitor acted dishonestly in prime-bank and high-yield transactions
Appropriate costs orders for privilege rulings and adjournment

enrichment.short_title: Taylor v Lancashire: Article 14 challenge to agricultural holdings enforcement scheme
key_facts: Joseph Taylor, tenant of Pollards Farm since 1962, faced possession after breaching an agricultural user covenant by processing and distributing milk off the holding.
He argued the 1986 Act discriminated under Article 14 because tenants facing Form 2 repair notices had stronger arbitration and tribunal protections than Form 3 tenants including user-covenant cases.
The Secretary of State intervened; Stanley Burnton J had ordered possession subject to human rights issues.
The tenant sought a declaration of incompatibility though he could not benefit from the specific repair/improvement distinction on which he relied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Tenant's appeal against possession order raising Article 14 ECHR read with Articles 6, 8 and Protocol 1 Article 1 and a section 4 HRA declaration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no declaration of incompatibility; possession order stands.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant may not obtain a declaration of incompatibility based on discrimination from which he cannot benefit where he is not a victim under section 7 HRA; differential routes under Case D depend on the covenant breached, not status or property, and are objectively justified by the long-standing distinction protecting tenants from oppressive repair notices.
legal_issues: Standing to seek a declaration of incompatibility for discrimination not affecting the claimant
Whether Form 2 and Form 3 regimes discriminate on property or status under Article 14
Objective justification for different agricultural holdings enforcement routes
Use of Hansard and departmental materials in compatibility review

enrichment.short_title: R v Allsopp: cocaine conspiracy appeals on RIPA and cell-site evidence
key_facts: Four defendants were convicted after retrial of conspiracy to supply cocaine between June 2001 and January 2002, linking north-east distributors to a London supplier.
Central evidence included covert recordings from a mobile-telephone listening device in Allsopp's car, surveillance, telephone billing and cell-site analysis.
Defences challenged RIPA authorisations, alleged unlawful interception, late disclosure of cell-site expert evidence, and co-conspirator hearsay against Wolf.
Allsopp received 12 years, Kelly and Wolf 10 years, West 8 years; West's sentence was reduced to 7 years on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals to the Court of Criminal Appeal against conviction and sentence after a retrial at Newcastle Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeals dismissed for all four appellants; sentence appeals dismissed except West's, reduced from 8 to 7 years.
enrichment.ratio: Covert in-car recordings of face-to-face conversations are not unlawful interceptions under RIPA where nothing passes through a telecommunications system; section 78 does not require disclosure of underlying RIPA suspicion material when statutory procedures and PII review are followed; marginally late cell-site expert evidence did not render convictions unsafe.
legal_issues: Admissibility of intrusive surveillance under section 78 PACE
Whether recorded car conversations were unlawful interceptions under RIPA
Prejudice from late disclosure of cell-site radius expert evidence
Admissibility of co-conspirator references against Wolf and Lucas directions on lies
linked_authorities: R v E [2004] EWCA Crim 1243

enrichment.short_title: Q v Q: footballer's surplus income sharing after McFarlane and Parlour
key_facts: After an 11-year marriage to a professional footballer, the parties agreed to an equal split of net capital but disputed implementation and income provision for the wife and four children.
The husband earned about £1.038 million net per annum; the wife sought 50% of net income for four years to build capital toward a clean break.
Capital issues included several properties, an R LLP tax scheme expected to yield £900,000, and T Limited company funds.
Following McFarlane v McFarlane; Parlour v Parlour the court had to fix the percentage share of surplus income over generously assessed needs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: First-instance financial remedies trial on capital division and periodical payments after decree nisi in a high-earner footballer divorce.
enrichment.outcome: Equal capital division ordered with balancing payment of £93,288 if the R LLP rebate materialises; child maintenance £20,000 per child; wife's maintenance £120,000; 40% of husband's net income for four years.
enrichment.ratio: Post McFarlane/Parlour, sharing surplus income over needs by periodical payments may facilitate a clean break, but a 50/50 split is not mandatory; fairness requires regard to children's priority claims, the wife's caring role, the husband's new partner and likely income decline, and section 25A's termination objective.
legal_issues: Implementation of equal capital division including mortgages and R LLP tax asset
Appropriate percentage of surplus net income for an extendable four-year term
Whether Parlour's 37.5% figure provides a binding guideline
Interaction of child maintenance, wife maintenance and savings toward clean break

enrichment.short_title: Coffey v Madonna publishers: strike-out of cherry-picked copyright work
key_facts: Claimant singer-songwriter Coffey alleged Madonna's 'Nothing Really Matters' infringed copyright in her song 'Forever After'.
She defined the copyright work as only the combination of vocal expression, pitch contour and syncopation around the phrase 'does it really matter'.
Defendants Warner/Chappell, record company and Leonard's publisher applied to strike out or obtain summary judgment.
Blackburne J held the pleaded work was not a separable musical work and largely comprised performance characteristics.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out re-amended particulars or for summary judgment in a copyright infringement claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim struck out under CPR Part 3.4(2)(a) and dismissed with costs; assessment of legally aided claimant's costs liability restricted.
enrichment.ratio: Copyright subsists in a work objectively determined by the court, not as cherry-picked features excised from a larger song; performance characteristics such as timbre and improvised pitch contour cannot constitute a separate musical work unless sufficiently separable from the composition.
legal_issues: Whether the pleaded combination of vocal features is a copyright musical work
Objective identification of the copyright work versus similarity by excision
Strike-out where claimant would not amend to rely on the whole song
Distinction between composition and performance for copyright purposes

enrichment.short_title: Spink v Wandsworth: disabled children's home adaptations and means testing

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970
Housing, Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Health and Social Services and Social Security Adjudications Act 1983

key_facts: Henry and Freddie Spink, severely disabled brothers, needed expensive home adaptations; their parents refused to disclose financial information to Wandsworth Council.
The council contended it need not fund adaptations until satisfied the parents could not reasonably pay; parents argued section 2 CSDPA imposed an unconditional duty.
A disabled facilities grant application had failed years earlier because of means-testing; the council also provided over £60,000 annual personal care.
The Secretary of State for Education and Skills intervened on the charging and statutory interpretation issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review appeal on whether parental means may be considered before providing section 2 adaptations and whether the council may recoup costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; council may have regard to parental means before deciding necessity; services provided via Children Act functions are subject to section 29 recoupment powers.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 28A, disabled children's section 2 duties are performed through Children Act Part III functions, permitting charges under section 29; following Barry, a local authority may treat adaptations as unnecessary if parents with sufficient means can reasonably be expected to fund them, though Article 3/8 obligations may arise in neglect cases.
legal_issues: Whether section 2 CSDPA creates an unconditional duty to fund adaptations for disabled children
Interaction of CSDPA, Children Act and HASSASSA charging provisions
Relevance of parental financial resources to 'necessity' under section 2
Availability of disabled facilities grants and recovery of expenditure

enrichment.short_title: Re Loftus estate: administratrix removed after disputed family settlement
key_facts: Ivor Loftus died intestate in 1990 leaving six children and assets including a company shareholding, 13 Gordon Road and a commercial yard.
Margaret took letters of administration and allegedly agreed a May 1992 pavement compromise giving her the yard and sale proceeds while siblings kept other assets.
Margaret assented the yard to herself, mortgaged it, and in 1999 transferred it to her son Dexter for £30,000; siblings claimed breach of trust and knowing receipt.
Long-delayed proceedings sought Margaret's removal, an account, and reconveyance of the yard from Dexter.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of beneficiary claims to remove administratrix, recover trust assets and determine limitation, estoppel and bona fide purchaser defences.
enrichment.outcome: No compromise agreement found; limitation and laches defences rejected; Margaret removed and ordered to account; Dexter held not to have purchased in good faith and must reconvey the yard and account for profits.
enrichment.ratio: Beneficiaries' claims to an intestate share fall within section 22(a) with time running from at least the end of the executor's year, or alternatively within section 21(1)(b) without limitation; an administratrix who converts estate assets and transfers them to her son with notice of beneficiary interests breaches trust and the son cannot rely on bona fide purchaser protection.
legal_issues: Whether a May 1992 family compromise agreement existed
Applicable limitation period for claims against an administratrix and converted trust property
Whether Dexter was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Removal of personal representative under section 50 Administration of Justice Act 1985

enrichment.short_title: Batayav v SSHD: Russian prison conditions and Article 3 country guidance
key_facts: Mr Batayav, a Tuvan Russian, refused military service in Chechnya, was imprisoned and fled to the UK claiming Article 3 protection against return to Russian custody.
His sole remaining claim was that general prison conditions inevitably breach Article 3, following earlier remittal after Kalashnikov v Russia.
On remittal the IAT found overcrowding was no longer a major universal problem and that disease risk did not establish a real risk for him personally.
The determination was designated country guidance; the appellant sought to adduce fresh expert evidence on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal challenge to a country guidance Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision on remittal concerning Article 3 and Russian prison conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; country guidance finding that post-Kalashnikov improvements mean return to serve a sentence does not necessarily violate Article 3 upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where Article 3 is claimed on systemic prison conditions rather than individual targeting, the applicant must show a consistent pattern of gross and systematic violations; the IAT's evaluation of post-Kalashnikov country evidence is a fact-finding exercise reviewable only for legal error, and country guidance determinations require rigorous but not exhaustive line-by-line rebuttal of every adverse report.
legal_issues: Whether Russian prison overcrowding remains an Article 3 breach after Kalashnikov
Standard of review for country guidance IAT decisions after S v SSHD
Effect of counsel's concession on overcrowding before the tribunal
Admissibility of fresh expert evidence on appeal
